name: Biblical Economics, Generosity, and Wealth

objectives.text: Identify that God made and owns everything, including the things people have
Demonstrate sharing materials and snacks with classmates and name a Bible verse that calls giving good
Explain that money is a tool people use to get what they need and to help others
Recall that God gives his people their daily bread and provides what they need
Retell the story of the widow's offering and explain why Jesus praised her small gift
Identify stealing as breaking the eighth commandment and name ways to respect the belongings of others
Describe how believers in Scripture brought tithes and offerings to support worship and ministry
Explain what Paul means when he says the love of money is a root of all kinds of evil
Explain stewardship as managing money and possessions that belong to God and giving account to him for their use
Explain what the parable of the rich fool teaches about trusting in possessions
Apply proverbs about honoring God, saving, and planning ahead to divide a sample allowance among giving, saving, and spending
Compare greed with contentment using the tenth commandment and Paul's example
Describe how the gleaning laws of Israel provided for the poor, the widow, and the stranger
Explain what Scripture teaches about borrowing, lending, and the burden of debt
Distinguish honest gain from dishonest gain using biblical laws and proverbs about just weights and fair dealing
Analyze the sharing of the early church in Acts and distinguish voluntary generosity from compelled redistribution
Explain the principles of willing, proportional, and cheerful giving in Paul's collection for the Jerusalem saints
Interpret Jesus' teaching about treasure in heaven and his warning that no one can serve both God and money
Analyze the accounts of the rich young ruler and Zacchaeus to compare how each responded to Jesus regarding wealth
Explain how the Reformed tradition connects generosity with trust in God's fatherly providence over riches and poverty
Explain how the eighth commandment protects private property and what duties toward the wealth of others the catechisms say it requires
Analyze the sabbath year and Jubilee laws for what they reveal about God's ownership of the land and his concern for the poor
Analyze the prophetic and apostolic condemnations of economic oppression, including withheld wages and exploitation of the poor
Construct a personal budget that applies biblical principles of giving, saving, avoiding unwise debt, and providing for one's household
Evaluate socialism and capitalism using biblical teaching on property, the poor, and human sinfulness
Defend from Scripture the obligation to care for the poor and distinguish the roles of the individual, the family, and the church's deacons
Evaluate the claims of the prosperity gospel against Scripture's teaching on godliness, contentment, and suffering
Create a written biblical theology of wealth that traces possessions through creation, fall, redemption, and consummation and applies the charge to the rich in 1 Timothy

changes: Kept and reworded the real competencies (God owns everything, sharing, money as a tool, tithing, love of money, stewardship, greed and contentment, debt, Mammon, generosity and trust, private property, budgeting, economic systems, care for the poor, wealth and kingdom purposes). Replaced vague verbs like Observe and Synthesize with observable ones and turned the final objective into a concrete written theology. Dropped the Parable of the Talents because it belongs to the sibling sub-topic on stewardship of talent. Added the widow's offering, daily bread, rich fool, gleaning laws, honest gain, Acts sharing, Paul's collection, rich young ruler and Zacchaeus, Jubilee, prophetic critique of oppression, and the prosperity gospel. Added catechism anchors for the eighth and tenth commandments, providence, daily bread, and the communion of saints.
